summary: An experimental document that defines the basic mechanisms of Photuris, a session-key management protocol used to set up shared secret keys between two parties.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people who have never met need to agree on a secret code without anyone overhearing. Photuris is a set of steps for doing that.

questions: what is a photuris cookie exchange
subtitle: A Diffie-Hellman based protocol for setting up short-lived IPsec session keys, with cookies to blunt flooding.

tldr.problem: IP Security (AH and ESP) needs keys, but long-lived configured secrets such as passwords are a poor thing to use directly for protecting traffic. Key setup also has to resist cheap flooding with bogus requests.
tldr.mechanism: Photuris runs over UDP in phases. A cookie exchange guards against flooding, a Diffie-Hellman value exchange creates a shared secret, an identification exchange checks who is who using existing secret keys, and later messages create, update or delete SPIs and their session keys.
tldr.outcome: The session keys never cross the Internet and replace the long-lived secrets for protecting traffic. RFC 2522 is an Experimental specification of the basic mechanisms, and the authors expect new data types and behavior to follow.

today: RFC 2522 is an Experimental specification, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the basic mechanisms; the text expects extensions and companion documents for further attributes.

sections.title: What Photuris Does
sections.content:
Photuris establishes short-lived session keys between two parties without passing those keys across the Internet. They directly replace the long-lived secret keys (passwords and passphrases) that were historically configured for security. It is intended for use with the IP Security protocols AH and ESP, and this document defines the basic mechanisms.

The basic protocol still uses previously configured secret keys, but only to identify the parties. The RFC says this is meant to speed deployment and reduce configuration changes. It mainly targets implementers and does not define service or application interfaces. It also warns that example values are for teaching and should not be assumed current or complete.

Two kinds of state result, each with its own lifetime: the Exchange LifeTime of the exchange itself (typically 10 minutes to one day, default 30 minutes), and a SPI LifeTime for each Security Parameters Index (SPI) the exchange creates (typically 2 to 30 minutes). When an exchange value expires, SPIs already derived from it are not affected, so traffic continues while a new exchange runs. The security of the whole thing depends on the quality of each party's random numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Photuris is a way for two computers to make a fresh secret code each time, so they do not need to keep using the same old password.

sections.title: The Four Phases
sections.content:
All messages travel in UDP, and the Initiator sends to UDP destination port 468. The Responder swaps addresses and ports in its replies. The UDP checksum must be correct, and a message with a bad checksum is silently discarded. The Initiator is responsible for recovering from all message loss by retransmission, and either party may start an exchange at any time.

  1. Cookie exchange. The Initiator sends a Cookie_Request. The Responder answers with a Cookie_Response containing its cookie and a list of offered Exchange-Schemes, and creates no state yet. This guards against flooding with bogus IP sources or UDP ports.
  2. Value exchange. The Initiator picks a scheme and sends its Exchange-Value and offered attributes in a Value_Request. The Responder replies with its own value and attributes. Each side computes the shared secret.
  3. Identification exchange. Identity_Request and Identity_Response identify the parties using configured secret keys, verify the earlier values, and carry each side's SPI and chosen attributes. These are masked with a privacy key derived from the shared secret, which hides identities and attribute values.
  4. SPI messages. Afterwards, SPI_Needed and SPI_Update can change session keys and create or remove SPIs.

The first three phases must complete in full before any Security Association can be used.
sections.plainLanguage: First they check each other is really there. Then they swap puzzle pieces to build a secret. Then they prove who they are in a whisper, and finally they can change the code whenever they like.

sections.title: Cookies, SPIs and Session Keys
sections.content:
A cookie must depend on the specific parties, must be impossible for anyone but the issuer to generate, and must be quick to produce and check. The RFC recommends a cryptographic hash such as MD5 over a local secret plus addresses and ports. The Responder does not cache its cookie, so it keeps no state during the initial cookie exchange, and regenerates it to validate a Value_Request.

Each party chooses the SPI for traffic it will receive. Per-direction session keys come from running the Key-Generation-Function over the cookies, both sides' generation keys, the Verification field and the shared secret. Because the order differs by direction, the keys usually differ too.

SPI_Needed asks the peer for an SPI with particular attributes. SPI_Update, sent by the SPI owner, can create an SPI (LifeTime and SPI both non-zero), delete one (LifeTime zero) or, with both zero, delete all SPIs for this association and mark the exchange expired. It cannot modify an existing SPI. An SPI should be refreshed after enough data, when anti-replay sequence numbers run out, or when its LifeTime expires, and an automated update can be set by default at half the LifeTime.
sections.plainLanguage: A cookie is a stamp that proves you really sent the request, so strangers cannot flood a computer with fake ones. Each computer picks its own mailbox number, and the keys for each direction are built from the shared secret.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman and the Basic Schemes
sections.content:
Photuris is based on Diffie-Hellman modular exponentiation. A party publishes g raised to x, mod p and both sides compute g raised to xy, mod p as the shared secret. The modulus and generator come from the Exchange-Scheme: offered in the Cookie_Response and chosen in the Value_Request. Every implementation must support moduli up to 1024 bits. The RFC gives its estimates as 64 bits of cryptographic strength for 512-bit moduli and 80 to 98 for 1024-bit moduli. Only generator 2 is required.

Exponents must not be small. If a chosen Exchange-Value uses fewer than half the modulus bits, or equals p-1, a new random exponent must be picked, and a received value that fails the requirements is silently discarded. Learned moduli must pass at least one probable-primality check before they are offered on.

The one required scheme is number 2. It is any modulus with generator 2, with the MD5 Hash as key-generation function, Simple Masking (XOR with the privacy key) as privacy method, and an MD5-IPMAC check for validity. Scheme numbers 3 to 255 are reserved for future published schemes, 256 to 32767 for vendor-specific ones, and 32768 to 65535 for private schemes. The required MD5-IPMAC attribute covers both symmetric identification and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side mixes a private number into a public one. They swap the mixed results, mix again, and both end up with the same secret, even though anyone listening only saw the mixed results.

sections.title: Error Messages and Silent Drops
sections.content:
Four error messages are defined, and none are masked. Bad_Cookie says the receiver-specific cookie is invalid or the exchange state has expired. Resource_Limit says too many SPIs or exchanges are in use, and the Initiator should double its retransmission timeout. Verification_Failure reports a failed identity or validity check and has no effect on the protocol itself beyond logging and notifying an operator. Message_Reject reports an unsupported optional message type or an unrecognized optional field.

Receivers must check that the cookie pair in an error message matches one in use, or the messages could be used for denial of service. Many other problems, such as a bad UDP checksum, an invalid cookie in a response, or a defective Exchange-Value, simply cause the message to be silently discarded. Implementations should log such events and notify an operator as appropriate. An Initiator that exceeds its retransmissions after seeing Bad_Cookie or Resource_Limit should start over with a new Cookie_Request.
sections.plainLanguage: If something is wrong, a computer either sends a short note saying what went wrong or just ignores the message, so a prankster gets nothing useful back.

sections.title: Defaults and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The specification has few tunable parameters. Defaults are 3 retransmissions, an initial retransmission timeout of 5 seconds, an Exchange TimeOut of 30 seconds, an Exchange LifeTime of 30 minutes (at least twice the timeout) and an SPI LifeTime of 5 minutes (at least three times the timeout). Each party also configures its known identities and secret keys, and local policy deciding what access each identity gets.

The security considerations section is candid. Photuris was built from available tools by network protocol designers with an interest in cryptography, rather than by cryptographers with an interest in network protocols. The document therefore carries only minimal cryptologic rationale, and the authors expect design decisions to be analysed and debated for years. Cryptologic details are left to separate documents that can be updated more readily.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say plainly that they are network people who borrowed cryptography tools, and that they expect experts to keep checking and improving the design.

messages.label: Value_Request
messages.note: Picks scheme, offers value and attributes.

messages.label: Value_Response
messages.note: Offers value and attributes; both compute the shared secret.

messages.label: Identity_Request
messages.note: Masked; makes SPI, identifies and authenticates.

messages.label: Identity_Response
messages.note: Masked; then session keys are made in each direction.

fields.name: Initiator-Cookie
fields.desc: 16 bytes. Identifies the exchange from the Initiator's side.

fields.name: Responder-Cookie
fields.desc: 16 bytes. Identifies the exchange from the Responder's side.

fields.name: Message
fields.desc: 1 byte. Each message type has a unique value.

items.label: Cookie_Response
items.desc: Returns the Responder cookie and offered schemes.

items.label: Value_Request
items.desc: Chosen scheme, Initiator Exchange-Value and attributes.

items.label: Identity_Request
items.desc: Identification, SPI and attribute choices, masked.

items.label: SPI_Needed
items.desc: Asks for an SPI with particular attributes.

items.label: Bad_Cookie
items.desc: Cookie invalid or exchange state expired.

items.label: Resource_Limit
items.desc: Too many SPIs or exchanges, or another resource is unavailable.

items.label: Message_Reject
items.desc: Unsupported optional message or unrecognized field.
